Internship

How I spent the summer of 2026.

JUL —
SEP 2026
Finance & Procurement Analyst Intern
Porsche Auto Investment Group (PAIG) · Hangzhou

PAIG operates more than 40 luxury dealerships across China, spanning Porsche, Bentley, Lamborghini, BMW and Audi. This summer I interned with the finance & procurement team in Hangzhou, and most of my work came back to one question: how do you turn data scattered across dealerships and suppliers into information management can actually make decisions with?

My biggest project was the quarterly AVB penetration-rate report. The raw data was each dealership's monthly sales export; from there I built a full reporting system — heatmaps and dealer rankings in Excel and Python, plus a 13-sheet workbook documenting the methodology — and later turned it into an interactive HTML dashboard the team can update whenever new data comes in. The most important detail: penetration has to be weighted by volume. A simple average across dealerships quietly skews the result.

I was also part of one of the department's most important procurement tenders this year, covering window tint, paint protection film and car wash & detailing services across the group's dealerships. I joined the meetings and pricing discussions with suppliers in each category, and owned the data for the first of three bidding rounds — compiling and comparing every supplier's quote, then turning the results into visuals presented to the suppliers.

Beyond that, I built a monthly Pareto analysis of procurement spend, which showed the top 20% of dealerships accounting for roughly 80% of it. I also put together a quote comparison for a partnership with ride-hailing companies, followed up on rebate agreements and frame-contract compliance, and helped write the H1 2026 procurement newsletter. Toward the end of the internship, I started designing an internal dashboard to bring AVB penetration, towing-service SLA, procurement data and CNR12 quarterly check reports onto a single platform.

02

Research

Undergraduate research in progress.

OCT 2026 —
NOW
Undergraduate Researcher
Learning Nonlinear Firm Exposures to Federal Reserve News · with Natanael Alpay (UCI Mathematics)

When the Fed makes an announcement, every stock hears the same news — but they don't all react the same way. Firms with more debt, less cash or higher market exposure should feel a rate surprise differently. The question my research partner Natanael Alpay and I are asking: using only what was known before each FOMC announcement, can a small, structured neural network predict which firms react more or less strongly — and does it hold up on later announcements better than a strong regularized linear benchmark?

The design covers 175 scheduled FOMC statements from 2004 to 2025 and up to 1,000 liquid U.S. stocks per event, using 30-minute returns around each announcement and eight pre-event firm characteristics such as leverage, cash and market beta. Fed news is summarized by the first three principal components of nine interest-rate changes. The network nests the elastic-net benchmark, so any improvement can only come from nonlinearity, and events are split by time — train on 2004–2013, tune on 2014–2017, and evaluate once on 2018–2025 — so the test is genuinely out of sample.

I'm responsible for the event calendar, data joins, accounting checks and the linear benchmark. We're discussing the project with Prof. Eric T. Swanson (UCI Economics) as a prospective faculty mentor, applying for UCI's UROP research funding, and aiming to present at the UROP symposium in spring 2027. It's at the proposal stage, so there are no results yet — and a clear null result would still be worth reporting.

Campus Activities

What keeps me busy at UC Irvine outside of class.

APR 2026 —
NOW
Director of Finance
Chinese Students & Scholars Association (CSSA)

CSSA brings together UCI's Chinese-speaking student community — 200 to 300 members — and puts on large-scale cultural events, from our annual Spring Festival Gala to campus events that draw more than 2,000 people. As Director of Finance, every funding request in the organization crosses my desk.

We manage an annual budget of more than $100,000, so the job is mostly trade-offs: forecasting what each event will really cost, deciding how to split funding across departments, and bringing budget-vs-actual numbers to our ten-person board so decisions get made on real figures rather than hopeful ones.

SEP 2025 —
MAR 2026
Learning Assistant
Department of Mathematics · Math 2A, Math 9 & Math 198

I supported three very different classrooms. Math 2A is introductory calculus, where first-year students build the foundation for everything that follows. Math 9 is the introduction to MATLAB and Python, where many of them write their first real code. And Math 198 takes UCI students into local high schools to teach math. Across the three, I worked with more than 200 students, from high schoolers to college freshmen.

In Math 9 that often meant sitting next to someone and tracing why a loop or a matrix operation wasn't doing what they expected. In 2A and 198 it meant finding a second or third way to explain the same idea until it landed — and adjusting how I taught it depending on who was in front of me.

Each week I gathered what I was hearing from students and compared notes with the other learning assistants, then brought the instructors concrete suggestions: which topics needed more time, which examples weren't working, and what to change in the next lab or problem set. Those notes fed directly into how later lessons and assignments were planned.
